strengths: Introduces the first comprehensive multiview video change detection benchmark (SceneDiff) with dense instance-level annotations, filling a major gap in the community's dataset landscape.
Proposes a robust, training-free pipeline that elegantly integrates recent 3D, segmentation, and semantic foundation models for zero-shot multiview change detection.

Demonstrates excellent empirical results, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches (such as CYWS-3D and 3DGS-CD) by a massive margin on both the proposed benchmark and the established RC-3D dataset.
Defines and thoroughly visualizes rigorous evaluation protocols, covering both per-view and per-scene metrics (including change type classification).
Provides a real-world physical robotic tidying application using an xArm 7 robot, validating the practical utility of the proposed method.
The manuscript is highly polished, well-written, and includes extensive ablation studies, failure case analyses, and a detailed appendix.
weaknesses: High computational latency: Taking nearly 160 seconds per sequence pair on an NVIDIA A40 GPU makes the current pipeline less suitable for real-time or interactive online applications.

Strong dependency on the quality of underlying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (e.g., $\pi^3$, VGGT). If the geometric alignment fails due to low overlap or textureless surfaces, the change detection quality drops drastically.
Limited discussion on how the pipeline can be made robust against severe illumination changes, which are shown to degrade both DINOv3 appearance matching and depth prediction.

strengths: Important and Highly Relevant Task: Multiview object-level change detection is a crucial capability for real-world applications like robotics and monitoring, but has been severely limited by the lack of realistic benchmarks and robust methods.

High-Quality Benchmark: SceneDiff Benchmark introduces 350 real-world, diverse, manually annotated video pairs (over 1,000 objects annotated with dense segmentation masks propagated via SAM2). It fills a major gap in existing benchmarks, which are either synthetic, have near-identical viewpoints, or lack instance-level annotations.

Novel and Elegant Methodology: The proposed SceneDiff method is an intuitive, training-free framework that effectively leverages modern foundation models. By using a feed-forward 3D model (π3) to co-register sequences and combining geometric/appearance cues with SAM segmentation regions, it elegantly avoids the sim-to-real gap and long optimization times of prior NeRF/3DGS-based approaches.

Strong Experimental Performance: The method dramatically outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches (such as CYWS-3D and 3DGS-CD) on both the new benchmark and the existing RC-3D dataset, indicating its high robustness across different scenarios.

Real-world Demonstration: Showing a practical downstream application with a robotic arm tidying up a table validates the usefulness and real-world transferability of the proposed change detection pipeline.
Excellent Writing and Visualization: The paper is exceptionally well-structured, clear, and provides a thorough ablation study and failure analysis in the main text and supplementary materials.
weaknesses: Upstream Dependency: As a training-free framework, the pipeline's performance is strictly bound by the accuracy of the underlying foundation models. If π3 fails to align the geometries or if SAM misses a region, the error cascades. Although this is a common limitation of modular zero-shot systems, it would be beneficial to discuss the specific error rates propagated from each upstream component.

Inference Latency: The average runtime of 159.4 seconds per sequence pair is relatively high, mostly dominated by generating mask proposals with SAM. This could limit its applicability in real-time robotic feedback loops where fast interaction is required.

Heuristics and Hand-tuned Thresholds: The framework relies on several hyper-parameters (e.g., weights in Eq. 4, merging thresholds, and co-visibility filters). While the validation analyses show reasonable robustness, adapting the method to highly distinct domains might require tedious parameter tuning.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging task: object-level change detection across different viewpoints in multi-view video sequences.
The introduction of the SceneDiff Benchmark with 350 video pairs and dense instance segmentation annotations fills an important gap in multiview change detection datasets.

The proposed method is training-free and successfully integrates several state-of-the-art foundation models (3D reconstruction, SAM, and DINO features) to achieve superior performance compared to existing baselines.
The authors demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed pipeline through a real-world robotic tidying demonstration.
weaknesses: Heuristic-Heavy Pipeline: The proposed method is highly dependent on a collection of hand-crafted heuristics and numerous hyperparameters (such as multiple lambda weights, various thresholds like \tau_{occ}, \sigma_{merge}, \tau_{sim}, and co-visibility percentages). The robustness and generalizability of these manually tuned parameters to significantly different environments are not fully discussed.

Lenient Evaluation Metric: The evaluation relies on a point-based metric where a prediction is counted as a true positive as long as its centroid falls within the ground-truth bounding box (and allows up to two predictions per ground truth without penalty). This metric is overly lenient and fails to measure the precision of object boundaries or scale estimation, which are critical for tasks like robotic manipulation.

Limited Algorithmic Novelty: Because the pipeline is training-free, the core technical contribution relies entirely on combining existing foundation models (SAM, \pi^3, DINO). The novelty lies more in the integration and engineering of these blocks rather than a fundamental algorithmic advancement.

Reproducibility Concerns: The method utilizes DINOv3 (reference [42]), which is not yet widely accessible or officially released. This poses a major reproducibility challenge for researchers trying to implement or compare against this work.

Inference Latency: At ~160 seconds per sequence pair (Table 6), the computational overhead is quite high, which may limit the method's applicability to real-time robotic loops or streaming applications.

strengths: High-Quality Benchmark: SceneDiff Benchmark fills a crucial gap in the literature by offering the first video-based multiview change detection dataset with instance-level annotations and consistent cross-view identity tracking across different camera trajectories.

Solid Training-Free Framework: The proposed SceneDiff algorithm elegantly combines modern foundation models for geometry (π³), segmentation (SAM), and semantic features (DINOv3) without requiring task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Exceptional Performance: The method achieves state-of-the-art results, showing massive improvements over existing methods on several benchmarks (SceneDiff, RC-3D, PASLCD, ChangeSim).

Extensive Ablations & Sensitivity Analysis: The paper presents thorough ablation studies analyzing different geometry backbones, feature extractors, and individual scoring components, demonstrating that the system is robust to hyperparameter variations.

Practical Robotic Demonstration: The authors show a real-world closed-loop robotic tidying application using a 7-DoF arm, which highlights the practical downstream impact of their change detection method.
weaknesses: Computational Overhead: Although significantly faster than 3DGS/NeRF-based approaches that require lengthy per-scene optimization, the method still takes around 159 seconds per sequence pair, which might limit its applicability in high-frequency real-time robotic loops.

Heavy Dependence on Foundation Models: The performance of SceneDiff is tightly coupled with the accuracy of the underlying models (e.g., π³, SAM, DINOv3). Failures in the early geometry estimation phase (such as in low-light, sparse views, or textureless scenes) directly compromise the alignment and final detection.

Minor Notation Inconsistencies: There are minor notation mismatches in Section 4.2. For example, Equations 1 and 2 use subscripts "before" and "after" (or " efore" and "\after"), whereas the text primarily refers to "pre" and "post" as defined in the task definition ($I_{pre}$ and $I_{post}$).

strengths: Introduction of the SceneDiff Benchmark: a highly valuable, first-of-its-kind multiview object-level change detection dataset featuring 350 video pairs with dense, consistent instance-level annotations and varying camera trajectories across 50 diverse scenes.

A clean, training-free algorithmic pipeline (SceneDiff) that elegantly combines state-of-the-art foundation models for 3D geometry extraction (pi^3), segmentation (SAM), and semantic features (DINOv3) to perform robust scene-level alignment and comparison.
The paper introduces rigorous, hierarchical evaluation metrics (px/im IoU, obj/im AP, obj/sc AP) that evaluate change detection from pixel-level quality up to scene-level cross-view consistency.

Excellent experimental results demonstrating that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing baselines (by up to 53% relative AP) on the proposed benchmark, as well as on RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim.
Demonstration of practical utility through a closed-loop real-world robotic tidying task, proving the system's readiness for downstream applications.
Thorough ablation studies, robustness analysis, and failure mode documentation presented in both the main paper and the extensive supplementary material.
weaknesses: High computational complexity and inference latency: At ~159.4 seconds per sequence pair, the method is relatively slow compared to lightweight 2D alternatives, which limits its applicability to real-time or resource-constrained scenarios.

Strong dependence on heavy foundation models: The performance of SceneDiff is bound to the reliability of pi^3, SAM, and DINOv3. Failures in any of these components (e.g., poor pose estimation due to low-co-visibility or textureless surfaces, or incorrect SAM segmentation) will lead to cascading errors in the final change detection.
Limitations in handling flat, thin, or extremely small objects where geometric cues (depth reprojection) are noisy or unreliable.

Ambiguity in complex, cluttered scenes containing highly repetitive items (e.g., supermarket shelves), where appearance-based region-matching (E_region) and reprojected features become less discriminative.

strengths: The paper introduces the SceneDiff Benchmark, the first multiview change detection dataset featuring dense instance-level annotations with consistent cross-view identity tracking under diverse camera trajectories. This fills an important gap in the change detection community.

The proposed SceneDiff method is training-free and elegant. It effectively leverages several state-of-the-art foundation models (SAM for segmentation, $\pi^3$ for 3D geometry, and DINOv3 for self-supervised semantics) to construct a robust pipeline.

The experimental evaluation is highly thorough, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks (the proposed SceneDiff, RC-3D, PASLCD, and ChangeSim). The relative performance improvements are substantial.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, providing clear explanations of the math, comprehensive ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, and a demonstration of practical utility on a real-world physical robotic platform.
weaknesses: The method is heavily reliant on the performance of individual foundation models. Systematic failures or errors in any of these components (such as failed pose estimation under low-overlap views, or noisy SAM mask boundaries) will propagate and degrade the final change detection performance directly.

The inference speed (159.4 seconds per sequence pair on an NVIDIA A40) is relatively slow. While it is faster than optimization-based 3DGS methods, it might still pose a latency bottleneck for real-time robotic operations.

The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited, as it primarily represents a pipelining and engineering assembly of pre-existing foundation models with threshold-based matching rules, rather than introducing a new learning paradigm.
